newsitem.title: USA: Release of Mexican gray wolves into U.S. West planned.
newsitem.headline: Release of Mexican gray wolves into U.S. West planned.

text.p: Federal wildlife officials on Thursday unveiled a plan to re-introduce the endangered Mexican gray wolf into Arizona and New Mexico despite protests from ranchers.

Nancy Kaufman, the Southwest regional director of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, told a news conference the federal agency plans to establish a population of 100 Mexican wolves in eastern Arizona's Apache National Forest and New Mexico's Gila National Forest by 2005.
"The wolf is a missing thread in the tapestry that is the West," Kaufman said. "This plan would restore part of the American natural heritage."

Before a single wolf is released the plan must undergo a 30-day public review period and win acceptance from Interior Secretary Bruce Babbit. If Babbit accepts the recommendation, as proponents believe he will, the first wolf release could take place by early 1998.
Five pairs of Mexican wolves are already being acclimatised to the wild in a New Mexico refuge.
Ranchers and agricultural organisations in New Mexico and Arizona opposed the plan and quickly attacked the Fish and Wildlife Service's official proposal on Thursday.
"This is a Big Brother issue," said Erik Ness, spokesman for the private New Mexico Farm and Livestock Bureau.
He claimed wolf reintroduction is a way for the federal government to increase its presence in the rural West. "This is a blatant attempt to take over more land."
Ranchers contended wolves pose a major threat to livestock and said they will challenge the plan in court.
Supporters responded by saying wolves mostly eat deer and ranchers will be fully compensated for any animals the wolves take.

From early this century Mexican gray wolves, a subspecies of the North American gray wolf, were hunted and trapped by the government and ranchers. They were eradicated from the wild in the United States by the early 1970s.
Five wolves were trapped in Mexico later that decade. Their offspring include 120 of the 149 living in zoos and sanctuaries across the United States.
